The company describes itself as providing \"Medical Software Solutions for an Accelerating World.\" It has approximately 20–21 employees and estimated annual revenue of ~$1.8M (per ZoomInfo/Bouncewatch, as of mid-2025). The CEO is Happy Dhani, who has a background in pharmacy (Pharmaneek Pharmacy) and healthcare services (Access Therapies Inc.). The CHPL contact is Leo Obrique, who has 30+ years of IT experience and holds a B.S. in Computer Science.\n     9→\n    10→Softbir operates multiple related brands/products:\n    11→- **CloudMD365** — the ONC-certified EHR product (now redirects to DocIndy)\n    12→- **DocIndy** — the current consumer-facing telemedicine brand (docindy.com)\n    13→- **iVisitDoc** — a telehealth platform and EMR system (ivisitdoc.com)\n    14→- **eMARneek** — electronic Medication Administration Record module\n    15→\n    16→The company appears to be a very small vendor with minimal web presence. The main website (softbir.com) contains almost no content — just a header with \"Medical Software Solutions.\" The CloudMD365 domain (cloudmd365.com) now 301-redirects to docindy.com. There is no evidence of a significant customer base, no third-party reviews on G2/Capterra/KLAS, and no case studies or press coverage. The company is unfunded (no disclosed investment rounds per Bouncewatch/Crunchbase).\n    17→\n    18→The social media handles reference \"pharmaneek,\" suggesting origins in the pharmacy/pharmaceutical space. The company appears to serve a dual role: developing healthcare software tools (the B2B side) and operating a direct-to-consumer telehealth service (the B2C side via DocIndy/iVisitDoc).\n    19→\n    20→## Product: CloudMD365\n    21→\n    22→CHPL ID: 10282\n    23→\n    24→### What It Is\n    25→\n    26→CloudMD365 is the ONC-certified health IT product from Softbir. Based on the abandoned trademark filing (Serial Number 90211494, filed September 2020), CloudMD365 is described as \"Software for patient/healthcare monitoring and management services, namely for use in Chronic Care Management (CCM)/Transitional Care Management (TCM), Diabetes Self-Management Training (DSMT), Remote Patient Monitoring (RPM), Electronic Medication Administration Record (eMAR), Electronic Health Record (EHR) and telemedicine.\" First use was reported as May 2018, with first use in commerce August 2019.\n    27→\n    28→The CloudMD365 domain now redirects to docindy.com, and the product appears to have been rebranded/subsumed into the DocIndy/iVisitDoc ecosystem. It is unclear whether \"CloudMD365\" still exists as a distinct product or whether the certification applies to the combined DocIndy/iVisitDoc platform.\n    29→\n    30→The certified criteria include:\n    31→- **(a)(1)–(a)(5)**: Core clinical data — CPOE for medications, labs, diagnostic imaging; demographics; problem list; medication list; medication allergy list\n    32→- **(b)(10)**: EHI export\n    33→- **(b)(11)**: Care plan — indicating the product supports care plan data\n    34→- **(d)(1)–(d)(13)**: Security and privacy criteria (authentication, encryption, auditing, etc.)\n    35→- **(g)(3)–(g)(5), (g)(7), (g)(10)**: Safety-enhanced design, quality management, accessibility, application access (FHIR API), standardized API\n    36→\n    37→Notably absent from the certification: (a)(9) clinical decision support, (a)(10) drug interactions, (a)(12)-(a)(14) family health history/patient-specific education/implantable device list, (b)(1)-(b)(3) transitions of care/clinical information exchange, (e)(1) patient portal/view-download-transmit, (f)(1)-(f)(7) public health reporting. This suggests a relatively limited clinical certification — core clinical data and FHIR API access, but not a full-featured EHR certification.\n    38→\n    39→### Users & Market\n    40→\n    41→The SED intended user description is simply \"Healthcare Provider.\" Based on the iVisitDoc EMR tour (which appears to be the clinical-facing version of this platform), the target users appear to be:\n    42→\n    43→- **Behavioral health / substance abuse treatment providers** — The EMR tour heavily emphasizes therapy session notes (SOAP, DAP formats), ICD-10 and DSM-5 diagnosis coding, treatment plans, pre-admission workflows, patient occupancy tracking across multiple locations, utilization review, rounds and security checks, homework planners, and aftercare management. This strongly suggests a behavioral health / residential treatment orientation.\n    44→- **Telehealth providers** — Psychiatrists, psychologists, therapists, social workers, general medicine physicians, dermatologists, and dietitians (per the provider FAQ).\n    45→- **Care coordinators** — For CCM/TCM programs, managing chronic conditions with Medicare billing codes (99490, 99487, 99489).\n    46→\n    47→No customer numbers, notable deployments, or market share data could be found. The company describes itself as providing \"Medical Software Solutions for an Accelerating World.\" It has approximately 20–21 employees and estimated annual revenue of ~$1.8M (per ZoomInfo/Bouncewatch, as of mid-2025). The CEO is Happy Dhani, who has a background in pharmacy (Pharmaneek Pharmacy) and healthcare services (Access Therapies Inc.). The CHPL contact is Leo Obrique, who has 30+ years of IT experience and holds a B.S. in Computer Science.\n\nSoftbir operates multiple related brands/products:\n- **CloudMD365** — the ONC-certified EHR product (now redirects to DocIndy)\n- **DocIndy** — the current consumer-facing telemedicine brand (docindy.com)\n- **iVisitDoc** — a telehealth platform and EMR system (ivisitdoc.com)\n- **eMARneek** — electronic Medication Administration Record module\n\nThe company appears to be a very small vendor with minimal web presence. The company appears to serve a dual role: developing healthcare software tools (the B2B side) and operating a direct-to-consumer telehealth service (the B2C side via DocIndy/iVisitDoc).\n\n## Product: CloudMD365\n\nCHPL ID: 10282\n\n### What It Is\n\nCloudMD365 is the ONC-certified health IT product from Softbir. Based on the abandoned trademark filing (Serial Number 90211494, filed September 2020), CloudMD365 is described as \"Software for patient/healthcare monitoring and management services, namely for use in Chronic Care Management (CCM)/Transitional Care Management (TCM), Diabetes Self-Management Training (DSMT), Remote Patient Monitoring (RPM), Electronic Medication Administration Record (eMAR), Electronic Health Record (EHR) and telemedicine.\" First use was reported as May 2018, with first use in commerce August 2019.\n\nThe CloudMD365 domain now redirects to docindy.com, and the product appears to have been rebranded/subsumed into the DocIndy/iVisitDoc ecosystem. It is unclear whether \"CloudMD365\" still exists as a distinct product or whether the certification applies to the combined DocIndy/iVisitDoc platform.\n\nThe certified criteria include:\n- **(a)(1)–(a)(5)**: Core clinical data — CPOE for medications, labs, diagnostic imaging; demographics; problem list; medication list; medication allergy list\n- **(b)(10)**: EHI export\n- **(b)(11)**: Care plan — indicating the product supports care plan data\n- **(d)(1)–(d)(13)**: Security and privacy criteria (authentication, encryption, auditing, etc.)\n- **(g)(3)–(g)(5), (g)(7), (g)(10)**: Safety-enhanced design, quality management, accessibility, application access (FHIR API), standardized API\n\nNotably absent from the certification: (a)(9) clinical decision support, (a)(10) drug interactions, (a)(12)-(a)(14) family health history/patient-specific education/implantable device list, (b)(1)-(b)(3) transitions of care/clinical information exchange, (e)(1) patient portal/view-download-transmit, (f)(1)-(f)(7) public health reporting. This strongly suggests a behavioral health / residential treatment orientation.\n- **Telehealth providers** — Psychiatrists, psychologists, therapists, social workers, general medicine physicians, dermatologists, and dietitians (per the provider FAQ).\n- **Care coordinators** — For CCM/TCM programs, managing chronic conditions with Medicare billing codes (99490, 99487, 99489).\n\nNo customer numbers, notable deployments, or market share data could be found. Given the company's size (~20 employees, ~$1.8M revenue), the customer base is likely very small.\n\n### Modules & Functionality\n\nBased on the iVisitDoc EMR tour page (ivisitdoc.com/emr-tour/), the ~$40–$142)\n\n**eMARneek (eMAR Module):**\n- Automates medication administration record keeping\n- Notifies nurses when it is time to reorder certain drugs\n- Bar code technology that verifies current quantities and dosages of every medication\n\n**Telehealth Services (Consumer-Facing):**\n- Video and messaging-based consultations\n- General medicine, mental health, dermatology, and nutrition {"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"toolu_01AjtdhmGNMkvwbrCw8Znu5D","type":"tool_result","content":"CloudMD365\n\nEHI Export Documentation\n\nIntroduction\nThis document provides a detailed guide on accessing, extracting, and interpreting patient\ninformation stored within an Electronic Health Information (EHI) file. This file is generated\nby the CloudMD365 system as part of its patient record export functionality. Specifically, the\nguide will cover:\n● File Format and Structure: An overview of the EHI file format, layout, and contents,\nwhich may include patient demographics, medical history, medications, treatment plans,\nand other relevant health records.\n● Extraction Process: Step-by-step instructions on how to download or retrieve the EHI file\nfrom CloudMD365, along with any tools or software needed for extraction.\n● Understanding Patient Information: Guidance on reading and understanding each\nsection of the EHI file, including tips for locating specific types of patient data and\ninterpreting any abbreviations or codes used within the document.\nThis document is intended for healthcare professionals, IT staff, or anyone responsible for\nmanaging patient records who requires a clear understanding of the EHI file generated by\nCloudMD365.\n\nFile Format and Structure\nThe Electronic Health Information (EHI) file exported from CloudMD365 is typically\nstructured in a standardized format, such as JSON or XML. This ensures compatibility with\nvarious health information systems and ease of use for data analysis and integration. Below\nare the key components and organization of the EHI file.\n\nFile Format\nThe EHI file is generally saved in either JSON (JavaScript Object Notation), which is a\nhuman-readable format that facilitates data exchange between systems.\nA JSON file may look like this:\nSample JSON Content\n{\n\n\fCloudMD365\n\nEHI Export Documentation\n\"patient\": {\n\"id\": \"123456\",\n\"name\": {\n\"first\": \"John\",\n\"last\": \"Doe\"\n},\n\"dob\": \"1990-01-01\",\n\"gender\": \"male\"\n}\n}\n\nKey Sections\n● Patient Demographics: Contains essential identifying details for the patient, including\nname, date of birth, gender, address, and contact information. This section ensures\naccurate patient identification and is critical for interoperability with other systems.\n● Health Summary: Provides a high-level overview of the patient's health status, including\nprimary diagnoses, chronic conditions, past surgeries, and relevant medical history. This\nsummary allows healthcare providers to quickly assess the patient’s overall health\ncontext.\n● Medications: Lists all prescribed and over-the-counter medications, including drug\nnames, dosages, and administration schedules. Information on medication history, start\nand end dates, and prescribing provider is also included.\n● Allergies: Documents known allergies, including medications, environmental factors, and\nfood allergens, as well as the severity of reactions. This section is essential for avoiding\nadverse drug interactions and ensuring patient safety.\n● Encounters: Records details of past medical visits, including encounter dates, visit types\n(e.g., in-person, telemedicine), reasons for the visit, diagnoses made, treatments\nprovided, and follow-up recommendations. This section helps in tracking the patient’s\nmedical history and continuity of care.\n● RPM Data (Remote Patient Monitoring): Contains data collected from remote patient\nmonitoring devices, such as blood pressure readings, glucose levels, heart rate, and\nother relevant metrics. This section is valuable for tracking patients’ health in real time,\nespecially those with chronic conditions requiring frequent monitoring.\n\nData Standards\nThe EHI file adheres to standards like HL7 FHIR to ensure interoperability, enabling the data\nto be integrated smoothly across different healthcare platforms.\n\n\fCloudMD365\n\nEHI Export Documentation\n\nExtraction Process\nTo successfully extract patient information from the EHI file generated by CloudMD365,\nfollow the steps outlined below:\n1. Log into CloudMD365\n● Access the CloudMD365 platform using your authorized credentials. Ensure that\nyou have the necessary permissions to access patient data.\n2. Navigate to the Export Functionality\n● Once logged in, from the menu bar, locate the Admin > Export Patient Health\nData. Then, select the patients to export data.\n3. Specify Export Options\n● Set the parameters such as data range for encounters to include in the export.\n4. Initiate the Export\n● Click the Export button to generate the EHI file. This may take a moment\ndepending on the amount of data being processed.\n5. Download the File:\n● Once the export is complete, a download link or prompt will appear. Click to\ndownload the EHI file to your local machine or designated storage location.\nStore the downloaded EHI file securely in compliance with data protection regulations (e.g.,\nHIPAA) to maintain patient confidentiality and data integrity.\n\nUnderstanding Patient Information\nThis section provides instructions on how to interpret the data within each part of the\nElectronic Health Information (EHI) file generated by CloudMD365. Understanding the\nstructure and content of each section is essential for healthcare providers and\nadministrative staff to accurately review patient information.\n\nPatient Demographics\nThis section contains basic identifying information about the patient, such as their name,\ndate of birth, gender, address, and contact details. It serves as a foundational reference to\nconfirm the patient’s identity and ensure that their medical records are accurately\nattributed.\nBelow table is the list of attributes with specified data type and short description.\n\n\fCloudMD365\n\nEHI Export Documentation\n\nPATIENT DEMOGRAPHICS\nField Name\n\nData Type\n\nShort Description\n\npatient_id\n\nGUID\n\nUnique identifier for the patient in the system\n\nfirst_name\n\nString\n\nPatient's first name\n\nlast_name\n\nString\n\nPatient's last name\n\ndate_of_birth\n\nString\n\nPatient's date of birth in YYYY-MM-DD format\n\ngender\n\nString\n\nPatient's gender\n\naddress\n\nObject\n\nObject containing address details for the patient\n\nemail\n\nString\n\nPatient’s email address\n\nADDRESS\nField Name\n\nData Type\n\nShort Description\n\nstreet\n\nString\n\nStreet address of the patient\n\ncity\n\nString\n\nCity of the patient’s residence\n\nstate\n\nString\n\nState of the patient’s residence\n\nzip_code\n\nString\n\nPostal or ZIP code of the patient’s address\n\nhome_phone\n\nString\n\nPatient's home phone number\n\nwork_phone\n\nString\n\nPatient's work phone number\n\nHealth Summary\nThe Health Summary section provides a high-level overview of the patient’s current and past\nhealth conditions. Patient Demographics** (10 fields)\n- patient_id (GUID), first_name, last_name, date_of_birth, gender, address (Object), email\n- Address sub-object: street, city, state, zip_code, home_phone, work_phone\n\n**2. Health Summary** (3 fields)\n- chronic_conditions (Array of Problem), diagnosis (Array of Problem), family_history (Array of String)\n- Problem sub-object: problem (String), icd_10 (String)\n\n**3. Medications** (5 fields)\n- medication (Array of Object), dosage, frequency, start_date, end_date\n\n**4. Allergies** (3 fields)\n- allergy, type, reaction\n\n**5. Encounters** (10 fields)\n- encounter_date, chief_complaint, diagnosis (Array of Problem), treatment, care_plan_goals (Array of String), care_plan_actions (Array of String), care_plan_followup, provider_id (GUID), provider_name, notes\n\n**6. RPM Data** (5 fields)\n- recorded_time, data_type, attribute_type, value (Float), unit\n\nTotal: ~36 fields across 6 entities (plus 2 sub-objects).\n\n### Data Standards\n\nThe document states the EHI file \"adheres to standards like HL7 FHIR to ensure interoperability\" — but there is no actual use of FHIR resource types, FHIR profiles, or FHIR-specific structure in the documented format. The JSON format shown is a custom/proprietary structure, not FHIR. The mention of FHIR appears to be aspirational or boilerplate rather than descriptive of the actual export.\n\n## Export Coverage Assessment\n\n### Data Domain Coverage\n\nThe product research reveals CloudMD365/iVisitDoc is a behavioral health-oriented EHR with telehealth, eMAR, care coordination, and billing capabilities. Comparing the documented export against what the product stores:\n\n**Covered domains:**\n- Patient demographics (basic — name, DOB, gender, address, contact)\n- Problem list / diagnoses (with ICD-10 codes)\n- Medications (with dosage, frequency, dates)\n- Allergies (type and reaction)\n- Encounters (date, complaint, diagnosis, treatment, care plan, provider, notes)\n- RPM data (remote monitoring vitals)\n- Care plans (goals, actions, follow-up — embedded in encounters)\n- Family history (as array of strings in health summary)\n\n**Missing or absent domains — significant gaps:**\n- **Billing data**: The product has integrated billing and CCM/TCM billing (Medicare codes 99490, 99487, 99489). None of this appears in the export. No charges, claims, payments, or billing codes.\n- **Behavioral health-specific data**: The product's core strength is behavioral health — therapy session notes (SOAP/DAP format), DSM-5 coding, treatment plans linked to patient journeys, assessment forms, outcome measures, homework planners, utilization review, pre-admission workflows, rounds/security checks. None of these specialty-specific data types appear in the export.\n- **Medication Administration Records (eMAR)**: The eMARneek module tracks medication administration with barcode verification, quantities, and reorder notifications. The export only includes prescribed medications, not administration records.\n- **Documents and attachments**: No mention of clinical documents, uploaded files, images (e.g., dermatology consultation images), or scanned records.\n- **Electronic signatures**: The product captures patient and guardian signatures. Not in the export.\n- **Patient-provided data**: Medical history disclosures, patient-uploaded images. Not in the export.\n- **Communication records**: HIPAA-compliant messages, telehealth visit records. Not in the export (encounters may capture visit metadata but not the communications themselves).\n- **Lab results**: Despite having a lab interface with 90+ testing partners and certified CPOE for labs (a)(1), there is no lab results section in the export. The encounters section might include some lab information in notes, but there is no structured lab data.\n- **Diagnostic imaging orders/results**: Certified for CPOE diagnostic imaging (a)(1) but no imaging data in the export.\n- **Insurance/enrollment information**: Not in the export despite verification of benefits being a product feature.\n- **Discharge planning and aftercare records**: Product features but absent from export.\n\n**The export covers roughly 6 clinical data categories out of ~15+ data domains the product manages.** The missing domains include both EHI-qualifying data (billing records, clinical documents, lab results, specialty assessments) and data that is clearly part of the designated record set (medication administration records, behavioral health assessments, treatment plans as standalone entities).\n\n### Export Format & Standards\n\nThe export uses a **custom JSON format** — not FHIR, not C-CDA, not any recognized healthcare standard. Despite the document claiming adherence to \"HL7 FHIR,\" the actual structure is a flat proprietary JSON with no FHIR resource types, no references, no coded terminologies beyond ICD-10, and no standard identifiers.\n\nThe format is simple and readable but lacks:\n- Standard terminology bindings (SNOMED, LOINC, RxNorm — only ICD-10 is mentioned)\n- Explicit value set definitions for coded fields (e.g., what are valid values for `gender`? `type` of allergy?)\n- Relationship/reference mechanisms between entities\n- Metadata (export date, system version, provenance)\n\nA third party could parse this JSON but would have limited ability to semantically interpret many fields without additional context.\n\n### Documentation Quality\n\nThe documentation is **minimal but clear**. It reads like a compliance artifact rather than a developer-oriented technical specification:\n\n- **Strengths**: Clean layout, field-level definitions with data types, a sample JSON snippet, step-by-step extraction instructions.\n- **Weaknesses**:\n  - No sample export file showing a complete patient record (the sample only shows a demographics fragment)\n  - No value set definitions for coded fields\n  - No specification of array element structure for some fields (e.g., medications says `medication` is \"Array of Object\" but the sub-fields are listed flat, not as object properties)\n  - No error handling or edge case documentation\n  - No versioning or change history\n  - The FHIR claim is misleading — the format is not FHIR\n  - No machine-readable schema (JSON Schema, OpenAPI, etc.)\n\nA developer could implement a basic import from this documentation but would encounter ambiguities around nested structures, coded values, and missing data handling.\n\n### Structure & Completeness\n\nThe field-level documentation covers **6 entities with ~36 fields total**. This is very sparse for an EHR that manages behavioral health patients. For comparison:\n- Demographics: 10 fields (reasonable for basics, but missing race, ethnicity, language, marital status, emergency contacts)\n- Health summary: 3 fields (very high-level — just lists of conditions and family history strings)\n- Medications: 5 fields (missing prescriber, pharmacy, NDC/RxNorm codes, route, status)\n- Allergies: 3 fields (missing severity, onset date, status)\n- Encounters: 10 fields (the most detailed section — includes care plan elements)\n- RPM: 5 fields (reasonable for vitals data)\n\nThere are no relationships between entities (e.g., which encounter prescribed which medication), no value sets documented, and no cardinality constraints.\n\n### (b)(10) vs (g)(10) Assessment\n\nThis is **not** a case of (g)(10) FHIR API documentation being repackaged as (b)(10). The export is genuinely a separate, proprietary JSON export mechanism accessed through the admin interface. However, it appears to cover approximately the same narrow scope of data that a basic USCDI/US Core export would cover (demographics, conditions, medications, allergies, encounters) — plus RPM data, which is a product-specific addition.\n\nThe fundamental problem is **breadth**: the export captures a patient clinical summary, not a comprehensive dump of all electronic health information the system stores about a patient. The behavioral health specialty data, billing records, medication administration records, lab results, documents, and communications are all absent. This is a significant gap for a (b)(10) requirement that mandates export of the entire designated record set.\n\n### Overall Assessment\n\nThis is a **minimal compliance effort** — a short PDF documenting a basic patient summary export. The documentation is honest (it doesn't overclaim) but severely incomplete relative to the data the product manages. The export appears to produce a JSON file containing a clinical summary of roughly the same scope as a C-CDA CCD, but in a proprietary format without standard terminologies.\n\nFor a ~20-employee company with a small customer base, this is not unusual — the documentation fulfills the letter of having *something* for (b)(10) while leaving significant data domains unaddressed. The 7-page PDF with ~36 field definitions is among the thinnest EHI export documentation in the CHPL ecosystem.\n\n## Access Summary\n- Final URL (after redirects): https://docindy.com/assets/CloudMD365%20EHI%20Export%20Documentation-Befwxq4M.pdf\n- Status: found\n- Required browser: no\n- Navigation complexity: direct_link\n- Anti-bot issues: none\n\n## Obstacles & Dead Ends\n\nNone.
